people.name: Phạm Văn Vy
body: When Phạm Văn Vy died in Minneapolis in April 2014, at 83, the Star Tribune called him a quiet community force. Its obituary says he did union work in South Vietnam, that he saved hundreds of people fleeing the country after the war, and that he later met with President Jimmy Carter. In the United States he continued that union work as a national organizer for the AFL-CIO and helped mediate a three-month textile workers' strike in Los Angeles.

In Minnesota he built institutions. MNopedia's chronology says he created the Vietnamese Community of Minnesota in 1981, with other first-wave arrivals, and became its first president. The group set out to preserve Vietnamese culture and to serve people spread across the Twin Cities. MNopedia also records ten presidents after him, the eleventh elected in 2023, so the organization has outlived its founder by more than a decade.

He also started what became Vietnamese Social Services of Minnesota, which identifies him as its founder and says he put up his own house as collateral. The Star Tribune says he chaired it for 25 years.

He also had a career inside the system. The obituary says he worked for 20 years in Hennepin County child protection services before retiring, and served on community commissions and advisory councils.
keyFacts: 1981: Created the Vietnamese Community of Minnesota and became its first president, by MNopedia's account.
1987: Vietnamese Social Services of Minnesota took that name; he put up his house as collateral.
Worked 20 years in Hennepin County child protection services.
Chaired Vietnamese Social Services of Minnesota for 25 years.
April 2, 2014: Died in Minneapolis at 83.

people.name: Bao Phi
body: Bao Phi was born in Vietnam in February 1975. By his own telling he was about three months old when his family was forced to leave. After refugee camps they settled in the Phillips neighborhood of South Minneapolis, which he has described as the city's largest, poorest and most racially diverse neighborhood at the time. He first performed a poem in the early 1990s on the South High School speech team, and his own site dates his career as a performance poet to 1991.

He became a two-time Minnesota Grand Slam champion and a National Poetry Slam finalist, and he appeared on HBO's Russell Simmons Presents Def Poetry. Coffee House Press published Sông I Sing in 2011 and Thousand Star Hotel in 2017. That same year he published the picture book A Different Pond, illustrated by Thi Bui, about a boy fishing before dawn with his father, a refugee who fishes to feed the family. In 2018 the book received a Caldecott Honor, the Charlotte Zolotow Award and the Minnesota Book Award for children's literature.

He spent nearly 23 years at the Loft Literary Center in Minneapolis, rising from receptionist to director of events and awards. There he created Equilibrium, a spoken-word series that pairs nationally known artists of color and Indigenous artists with Minnesota artists. In August 2022 he joined the McKnight Foundation, where, as of October 2026, he is a program officer for arts and culture.
keyFacts: February 1975: Born in Vietnam; his family later settled in Phillips, South Minneapolis.
2011: Sông I Sing published by Coffee House Press.
2017: Thousand Star Hotel and A Different Pond published.
2018: A Different Pond received a Caldecott Honor, the Charlotte Zolotow Award and a Minnesota Book Award.
August 2022: Joined the McKnight Foundation after nearly 23 years at the Loft.
people.connectToWork: A Different Pond shows a parent's work through a child's eyes. In the service you provide, what do you ask about how a family gets by, and what do you assume instead of asking?

people.name: Christina Nguyen
body: In June 2024 at the James Beard Awards in Chicago, the Best Chef: Midwest award went to Christina Nguyen of Minneapolis. The Twin Cities had three nominees that night, and she was the only one to win. She had been a semifinalist before and a finalist in 2020.

She told MPR News that her parents came as refugees and had to start their lives over from scratch. Her mother quit a safe job at 3M to open a printing and graphic design business, and Nguyen has said that growing up in that print shop made it seem normal for an Asian woman to start a business. She is a self-taught chef. After college she tried a boba shop and a clothing boutique. In 2011 she and her husband, Birk Grudem, started Hola Arepa as a food truck and later gave it a permanent home in south Minneapolis.
The couple then opened Hai Hai in Northeast Minneapolis, which serves Southeast Asian street food drawing on her upbringing and her travels. It has appeared on national lists of best new restaurants.
keyFacts: 2011: Launched Hola Arepa as a food truck in Minneapolis.
2020: James Beard finalist.
June 2024: Won the James Beard Award for Best Chef: Midwest for Hai Hai.

people.name: Viet-Hanh Winchell
body: The Minnesota Judicial Branch says Viet-Hanh Winchell is the first Vietnamese American state court judge in Minnesota. The governor announced her appointment in spring 2024, and the Judicial Branch dates it May 13, 2024. She succeeded retiring Judge Richard C. Ilkka in the Tenth Judicial District, which covers Anoka, Chisago, Isanti, Kanabec, Pine, Sherburne, Washington and Wright counties, and she sits in Stillwater.

AsAmNews reported that her parents fled Vietnam in 1979 with their three children and lived in a refugee camp in Thailand before coming to Minnesota, where she was born. She earned her bachelor's degree at the University of Minnesota and her law degree at Hamline University School of Law.

Before the bench she ran a solo practice handling criminal and civil matters and served as court-appointed counsel for parents in child protection cases. She served as president of the Washington County Bar Association, on the state Commission on Judicial Selection, and on the Washington County Children's Justice Initiative.
As of October 2026 she is the only candidate listed for her seat on the November 3, 2026 ballot. Her current term runs through January 2027.

May 13, 2024: Appointed to Minnesota's Tenth Judicial District, chambered in Stillwater.
Named by the Minnesota Judicial Branch as the state's first Vietnamese American state court judge.
Earlier served as court-appointed counsel for parents in child protection cases.
November 3, 2026: Listed as the only candidate for her seat.

people.name: Hoang Murphy
body: Hoang Murphy knows Minnesota's foster care system from the inside. Foster Advocates describes him as a Foster and a former high school English teacher. His Run for Something candidate profile describes him as a first-generation Vietnamese American.

In 2018 Murphy founded Foster Advocates, a St. Paul group centered on people with experience in foster care. It worked at the State Capitol on the Fostering Higher Education Act, passed in 2021, which by Sahan Journal's account covers the full cost of attendance at public, Tribal and most private colleges for eligible young people up to age 26.

Foster Advocates also lobbied for the 2022 law that created the state's Office of the Foster Youth Ombudsperson, and Murphy testified for the bill. That year he was named a Bush Fellow, and he ran for the Minnesota House in District 67A. He stepped down as executive director in 2023. As of October 2026 Foster Advocates lists him as its founder and as a continuing supporter, and Osahon Akpata-Tanious, who started in September 2025, is its executive director.

2021: Fostering Higher Education Act passed.

2023: Stepped down as executive director; named a Child Welfare Change Maker that year.

people.name: Viet Thanh Nguyen
body: In 1975, four-year-old Viet Thanh Nguyen arrived at Fort Indiantown Gap in Pennsylvania, one of the U.S. military bases turned into camps for Vietnamese refugees. He had been born in Ban Mê Thuột, in South Vietnam's central highlands, in 1971. He has described how families could leave the camps only when an American sponsor took them in. No sponsor would take his family of four, so his family was split up for a time.

His family eventually settled in San Jose, California, where his parents ran a grocery store. Nguyen became a scholar of literature and a professor at the University of Southern California. In 2015 he published his first novel, The Sympathizer, the story of a communist double agent living among South Vietnamese exiles in Los Angeles. It won the 2016 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. In 2017 he received both a MacArthur Fellowship and a Guggenheim Fellowship. HBO adapted The Sympathizer as a miniseries in 2024.
Through his novels, essays and nonfiction, Nguyen argues that refugees should be understood as full people with their own histories, not just as victims or as symbols of American generosity.

1975: Arrived as a refugee at Fort Indiantown Gap, Pennsylvania.
2015: Published The Sympathizer.
2016: Won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction.
2017: Awarded MacArthur and Guggenheim fellowships.
2024: HBO miniseries adaptation of The Sympathizer premiered.

people.name: Eugene H. Trinh
body: In the summer of 1992, the Space Shuttle Columbia launched with a physicist from Saigon aboard. Eugene Huu-Chau Trinh flew on STS-50 as a payload specialist for the first United States Microgravity Laboratory, a mission devoted to experiments in near-zero gravity. He became the first Vietnamese American to travel to space.

Trinh was born in Saigon on September 14, 1950. When he was two, his family moved to Paris, so his path to the United States was different from the refugee journeys that came later. He came to the U.S. for college, earned a bachelor's degree in mechanical engineering and applied physics from Columbia University in 1972 and a PhD in applied physics from Yale in 1977. He then worked at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, where he studied how fluids and droplets behave.
He went on to direct NASA's Physical Sciences Research Division.

1972: B.S., Columbia University.
1977: Ph.D. in applied physics, Yale University.
1992: Flew aboard STS-50 / USML-1 as a payload specialist, the first Vietnamese American in space.

people.name: Dat Nguyen
body: Dat Nguyen was born in 1975 at a refugee center in Arkansas, just after his family escaped South Vietnam during the fall of Saigon. They moved to Rockport, a fishing town on the Texas Gulf Coast, and his family worked in shrimping.

Nguyen became a linebacker at Texas A&M, where he set a school record with 517 career tackles. In his senior season he was named a unanimous All-American and won both the Chuck Bednarik Award and the Lombardi Award, two of college football's top defensive honors. The Dallas Cowboys drafted him in 1999. He became the first Vietnamese American to play in the NFL and was named second-team All-Pro in 2003.

A neck injury ended his playing career after the 2005 season. He later coached linebackers for the Cowboys (2007–09) and joined the Texas A&M staff in 2010 and 2011. In 2017 he was elected to the College Football Hall of Fame. He told his family's story in an autobiography, Dat: Tackling Life and the NFL.
keyFacts: 1975: Born at a refugee center in Arkansas; raised on the Texas Gulf Coast.
1998: Won the Bednarik and Lombardi Awards at Texas A&M; set a school record with 517 career tackles.
1999–2005: Played linebacker for the Dallas Cowboys, the first Vietnamese American in the NFL; second-team All-Pro in 2003.
2007–2011: Linebackers coach, Dallas Cowboys (2007–09), then Texas A&M staff (2010–11).
2017: Elected to the College Football Hall of Fame.

people.name: Anh "Joseph" Cao
body: On December 6, 2008, voters in New Orleans, a city still rebuilding after Hurricane Katrina, elected an immigration lawyer and former Jesuit seminarian to the U.S. House of Representatives. Anh Quang "Joseph" Cao became the first Vietnamese American, and the first person born in Vietnam, to serve in Congress.

Cao was born in Saigon on March 13, 1967. He left Vietnam as a child in 1975. His father, a South Vietnamese army officer, spent years in a communist "re-education" camp, one of the prison camps where former officers and officials were held after the war. Cao earned a physics degree from Baylor University in 1990 and then entered the Society of Jesus, hoping to work for social justice among the poor. He later chose law and opened an immigration practice in New Orleans, serving the Vietnamese community in the eastern part of the city. Katrina hit that community hard in 2005.

A Republican, Cao defeated nine-term Democratic incumbent William Jefferson, who was facing federal corruption charges. He served one term, from 2009 to 2011, in a heavily Democratic district, and was known for crossing party lines on some votes.

1975: Left Vietnam as a child; his father was held in a re-education camp.
1990: B.S. in physics, Baylor University; later a Jesuit seminarian, then an immigration attorney.
December 6, 2008: Elected to Congress from Louisiana's 2nd District.
2009–2011: Served as the first Vietnamese American member of Congress.

people.name: Stephanie Murphy
body: When Stephanie Murphy was about six months old, her family fled Vietnam by boat. The boat ran out of fuel and drifted at sea until, as her family has described it, the U.S. Navy found them and helped bring them to a refugee camp in Malaysia. A Lutheran church later sponsored the family's resettlement in Virginia.

Murphy was born in Ho Chi Minh City on September 16, 1978. She grew up in Virginia, graduated from the College of William & Mary, and earned a master's degree in foreign service at Georgetown University. After the September 11 attacks she worked as a national security specialist at the U.S. Department of Defense, then later in business and as a university instructor in Florida.

In 2016 she defeated longtime Republican incumbent John Mica, in a central Florida district. She became the first Vietnamese American woman elected to Congress. As a Democrat she served three terms, from 2017 to 2023, and was known for her work on defense and on bipartisan, fiscally moderate coalitions.

people.name: Kiều Chinh
body: Kiều Chinh was born in Hanoi in 1937 and moved south as a refugee at 17, beginning to act at 19. In 1975, when Saigon fell, she was already one of South Vietnam's most famous film stars. She had won South Vietnam's Best Actress Award in 1969 and Best Leading Actress at the 1973 Asia-Pacific Film Festival in Taipei. After the fall of Saigon she lost virtually everything and came to the United States as a refugee to start over.

Her official biography says the actress Tippi Hedren sponsored her, and that Hedren and actor William Holden helped her get back to work in Hollywood. She kept working for close to seven decades. Her credits now number more than 100 films and television shows, made in countries from the Philippines and Hong Kong to India, Australia and Canada. American audiences know her from M*A*S*H, China Beach, ER, NCIS: Los Angeles and the film The Joy Luck Club. She also appeared in Journey from the Fall, a film about the boat-people era, and in the 2024 HBO series The Sympathizer.

In 1996 a documentary about her return to Vietnam, Kieu Chinh: A Journey Home, won an Emmy Award. In 1993 she co-founded the Vietnam Children's Fund with Lewis Puller Jr. and Terry Anderson, both American Vietnam-era figures. The fund has built 51 schools in Vietnam. Her site says they serve more than 40,000 students a year; a 2017 Congressional Record tribute says more than 30,000. In 1990 the U.S. Congress named her "Refugee of the Year," and in 1992 she became the first Vietnamese woman invited to speak at the 10th anniversary of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial groundbreaking. In 2021 she published a memoir, Kieu Chinh – An Artist in Exile, in English, Vietnamese and French. As of October 2026 her site lists a lead role in the film Chrysalis, set for release that fall.

1969: Best Actress Award of South Vietnam.
1973: Best Leading Actress, Asia-Pacific Film Festival, Taipei.

1990: Named "Refugee of the Year" by the U.S. Congress.
1993: Co-founded the Vietnam Children's Fund (51 schools built).
1996: Emmy Award for the documentary Kieu Chinh: A Journey Home.
2021: Published her memoir Kieu Chinh – An Artist in Exile.

people.name: Ocean Vuong
body: Ocean Vuong's best-known novel is a letter from a son to his mother, a woman who cannot read in any language. That is close to his own family's story. The MacArthur Foundation describes Vuong as the child of illiterate rice farmers from rural Vietnam. Born in 1988 in Saigon (Ho Chi Minh City), he came to the United States as a refugee with his family when he was about two, after a brief stop in the Philippines, and grew up in Hartford, Connecticut, in a family of nail salon and factory workers.

Vuong studied at Brooklyn College of the City University of New York, graduating in 2012, and earned an MFA from New York University in 2016. He started with small chapbooks, Burnings (2010) and No (2013). His first full poetry collection, Night Sky with Exit Wounds, came out in 2016. In 2019 he published his first novel, On Earth We're Briefly Gorgeous, the letter to his mother. In it he writes about war, family violence, work, love between young men, and how trauma passes from one generation to the next.

His poems and essays have appeared in The New Yorker, The Atlantic, Poetry and other major magazines. According to the MacArthur Foundation, his work combines the oral storytelling and folklore of rural Vietnam with experimental English. In 2019, at age 30, he was named a MacArthur Fellow. He published a second poetry collection, Time Is a Mother, and a second novel, The Emperor of Gladness. As of October 2026 his own site lists him as Professor of Modern Poetry and Poetics in the MFA program at New York University.

c. 1990: Came to the U.S. as a refugee at about age two; grew up in Hartford, Connecticut.

2019: On Earth We're Briefly Gorgeous (novel).

people.name: Jacqueline H. Nguyen
body: On May 14, 2012, Jacqueline Hong-Ngoc Nguyen received her commission as a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. It is the largest federal appeals court in the country, covering California and much of the West. She was born in 1965 in Đà Lạt, a highland city in South Vietnam, and came to the United States as a refugee at age 10 after the fall of Saigon. San Francisco State University's Asian Pacific Islander American biography project describes her as the first Vietnamese American federal judge and the first Asian American woman to serve as a federal appellate judge.

The Federal Judicial Center's record shows a steady climb. Nguyen earned her bachelor's degree from Occidental College in 1987 and her law degree from UCLA School of Law in 1991. She worked in private practice in Los Angeles from 1991 to 1994. She then spent seven years as a federal prosecutor, an Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California, from 1995 to 2002, and was deputy chief of the office's General Crimes Division from 2000 to 2002.

In 2002 she became a judge of the Los Angeles County Superior Court, the state trial court for the county. On December 4, 2009, she was commissioned as a U.S. District Judge for the Central District of California. Less than three years later she was elevated to the Ninth Circuit. The Federal Judicial Center's record, checked in October 2026, shows no end date for that service. Her career covers all levels of the courts: private lawyer, prosecutor, state trial judge, federal trial judge and federal appeals judge.

1975: Came to the U.S. as a refugee at age 10.

2002–2009: Judge, Los Angeles County Superior Court.
December 4, 2009: Commissioned as U.S. District Judge, Central District of California.
May 14, 2012: Commissioned as Ninth Circuit judge.

people.name: Viet Xuan Luong
body: On the day before Saigon fell in 1975, nine-year-old Lương Xuân Việt and his family got out of Vietnam aboard the U.S. aircraft carrier USS Hancock. They came to the United States as political refugees and settled in Los Angeles. His father had been a senior South Vietnamese military officer. In America he worked as an armed security guard, and Luong's mother worked at a fast-food restaurant.

In 1983 Luong entered the University of Southern California on a full Army ROTC scholarship. He graduated in 1987 with a degree in biological sciences and became an infantry officer. His career took him to Haiti, Bosnia and Kosovo. He commanded a battalion of 82nd Airborne Division paratroopers in Iraq in 2007–08 and led the 101st Airborne Division's 3rd Brigade Combat Team in Afghanistan in 2010–11.

In 2014 Luong became the first Vietnamese-born officer in the U.S. military to reach the rank of general, pinning on the star of a brigadier general. By 2016 he was serving as deputy commanding general for maneuver of the 1st Cavalry Division, and the Carnegie Corporation of New York named him one of its Great Immigrants honorees. He later commanded U.S. Army Japan for three years as a major general and retired in June 2021 after 34 years in the Army.

1983–1987: USC on a full ROTC scholarship; B.S. in biological sciences.
2007–08: Commanded an 82nd Airborne battalion in Iraq.
2010–11: Led the 101st Airborne's 3rd Brigade Combat Team in Afghanistan.
2014: First Vietnamese-born U.S. military general officer.
2016: Carnegie "Great Immigrants" honoree.
June 2021: Retired as a major general after commanding U.S. Army Japan.

people.name: Dominic Mai Thanh Lương
body: On June 11, 2003, at St. Columban Church in Garden Grove, California, in the heart of Orange County's Little Saigon, Dominic Mai Thanh Lương was ordained a bishop. He was the first Vietnamese American Catholic bishop in the United States. Vietnamese Catholics had a long history behind them: many had fled from north to south Vietnam in 1954 and fled again in 1975.

Lương was born on December 20, 1940, in Minh Cường in northern Vietnam, about 50 miles from Hanoi. He was the second youngest of 11 children in a devout Catholic family. In 1956, at 16, his bishop sent him to the United States to continue his seminary studies. He did not see his family or homeland again until 1979. He was ordained a priest in Buffalo, New York, on May 21, 1966, for the Diocese of Đà Nẵng, but the war kept him from going home. He served as a hospital chaplain in Buffalo.

When Saigon fell in 1975, he worked with refugees in a camp on Guam. In 1976 he moved to New Orleans to direct the archdiocese's Vietnamese Apostolate, serving the many refugees settling there. He became founding pastor of Mary Queen of Vietnam parish in New Orleans East, which America Magazine describes as the first Vietnamese Catholic parish in the United States. From 1989 to 2003 he directed the National Pastoral Center for the Vietnamese Apostolate.

Pope John Paul II named him auxiliary bishop of Orange on April 25, 2003. His motto was "You are strangers and aliens no longer," from the Letter to the Ephesians. He retired in early 2016 and died on December 6, 2017, at age 77.
keyFacts: December 20, 1940: Born in Minh Cường, northern Vietnam.
1956: Sent to the U.S. at 16 for seminary studies.
May 21, 1966: Ordained a priest in Buffalo, New York.
1976: Began directing the Vietnamese Apostolate in New Orleans; later founded Mary Queen of Vietnam parish.
June 11, 2003: Ordained the first Vietnamese American Catholic bishop (auxiliary bishop of Orange).
December 6, 2017: Died at age 77.

people.name: Christine Ha
body: Christine Ha was born in Southern California in 1979 and spent most of her childhood in Houston. Her parents were Vietnamese refugees. In her third year of college, at about age 20, she began losing her sight. Doctors first thought it was multiple sclerosis. A few years later she was diagnosed with neuromyelitis optica, an autoimmune disease; Fox News reported the year as 2004. She is legally blind, and by her account in BrainHealth her limited vision has stayed about the same since 2007.

She kept cooking, in part to reconnect with her Vietnamese heritage. In 2012 she won season 3 of the U.S. television show MasterChef, as its first blind contestant, while finishing a graduate degree in creative writing. Her cookbook, Recipes from My Home Kitchen: Asian and American Comfort Food, came out in 2013. In 2014 she received the American Foundation for the Blind's Helen Keller Personal Achievement Award.

In July 2019 she opened The Blind Goat, a modern Vietnamese gastropub in Houston's Bravery Chef Hall, which was a James Beard semifinalist for Best New Restaurant in 2020. A second Houston restaurant, Xin Chào, followed.
keyFacts: 1979: Born in Southern California to Vietnamese refugee parents; raised mostly in Houston.
2004: Diagnosed with neuromyelitis optica, by Fox News's account, after a first diagnosis of multiple sclerosis.
2012: Won MasterChef (U.S.) season 3 as its first blind contestant.
2014: Helen Keller Personal Achievement Award, American Foundation for the Blind.
July 2019: Opened The Blind Goat in Houston.
people.connectToWork: When someone loses vision as an adult, what does your process assume about what they can no longer do? Who asks them what they want to keep doing, and what would you change in order to support it?

people.name: Ca Van Tran
body: Ca Van Tran and his wife Kim fled Saigon in 1975, after he had worked as an interpreter for the U.S. Marines and for USAID. In the U.S. he first worked as a janitor for $2 an hour, and over fifteen years the couple acquired four Mexican-American restaurants. After he returned to Vietnam in 1990 to visit his ailing father, they founded Vietnam Assistance for the Handicapped (VNAH) in 1991 to help war amputees and other disabled people, and in 1993 they founded a sister organization, HealthEd, for disadvantaged children.

VNAH's own page credits his advocacy with contributing to Vietnam's national disability law, and it says he and his family received death threats from both sides of the political divide. We found no independent account of his role in the law. VNAH's January 2026 fact sheet says it has supported 85,100 people with disabilities and trained 27,800 providers, civil servants and caregivers over 34 years. An undated VNAH page gives a different total, over 90,000 people given assistive devices.
keyFacts: 1975: Fled Saigon with his wife Kim.
1991: Co-founded VNAH.
1993: Co-founded HealthEd.
January 2026: VNAH reports supporting 85,100 people with disabilities over 34 years.
people.connectToWork: Some people will know disability as a rights question from work done in Vietnam or elsewhere. How would you find out what a person already knows about rights, instead of explaining them from the beginning?

institutions.name: Vietnamese Social Services of Minnesota
institutions.location: 277 University Avenue West, St. Paul, Minnesota
body: Thousands of Vietnamese refugees who had reached Minnesota by the 1980s needed help with jobs, English and health care. By the agency's own account, founder Vy Pham (Phạm Văn Vy) put up his own house as collateral, and in May 1987 it became Vietnamese Social Services of Minnesota.

VSS describes its work today as adult education and English classes, health programs and elder programs. It says it reaches more than 12,000 participants a year, about half of them Vietnamese and about 40 percent Karen. These figures are its own and do not say how a person is counted. Its Elder Circle program brings seniors together for wellness and recreation in parks and community spaces, with a People for Parks grant from the Minneapolis Parks Foundation.

Its own history lists the recognition it has received: the 956th Point of Light from President George H.W. Bush in 1992, the Minnesota Peace Prize in 1995, and the Asian Leadership Award from the Council on Asian-Pacific Minnesotans in 1997. Like other agencies started by refugees, it has widened its reach to newer arrivals, including Karen and Karenni people from Burma and East Africans from Somalia and Ethiopia.
keyFacts: May 1987: Became Vietnamese Social Services of Minnesota.
1992: Named the 956th Point of Light.
1995: Minnesota Peace Prize.
1997: Asian Leadership Award, Council on Asian-Pacific Minnesotans.
By its own count, more than 12,000 participants a year.
institutions.connectToWork: When you refer someone to a culturally specific agency, what have you checked about what it offers now, and how is that work paid for? What does your agency give back for the time it asks of them?

institutions.name: Chùa Phật Ân
aliases: Hội Phật Giáo Việt Nam tại Minnesota
body: The temple's own history says the Vietnamese Buddhist Association of Minnesota was formally founded on May 15, 1976, barely a year after the fall of Saigon. Its first base was the Bloomington home of its founding president. In October 1977 the association bought and converted a house on Dale Street in St. Paul.

In August 1983 it bought a church property at 475 Minnesota Avenue in Roseville and turned it into Chùa Phật Ân. Work on a main hall began in April 1989 and was dedicated in September 1991, and a new, larger hall was built on the grounds in 2012.

MNopedia calls it Minnesota's first Vietnamese temple and says that, like St. Joseph Hiển parish, it offered Vietnamese language classes to younger people on Sundays. It is not the only faith home for Vietnamese Minnesotans: the directory on this page lists Catholic parishes as well.
keyFacts: May 15, 1976: Association founded.
October 1977: Bought a house on Dale Street, St. Paul.
August 1983: Bought the Roseville property that became the temple.
1991 and 2012: Main halls dedicated and built.
institutions.connectToWork: Before you announce something through a place of worship, who has told you the person wants that connection? What other route do you offer to someone who does not belong there?

institutions.name: Little Saigon, Orange County
institutions.location: Westminster and Garden Grove, California, centered on Bolsa Avenue
body: By the 1970s, the Bolsa Avenue area of Westminster, California, was in economic decline. Then refugees began arriving after the fall of Saigon in 1975. Many of them opened businesses, and the businesses drew more Vietnamese families to settle nearby. The Center for Health Journalism calls it the largest Vietnamese enclave outside Vietnam.

Frank Jao, a refugee who opened Bridgecreek Development on Bolsa Avenue in 1978, worked with local officials on a plan to promote culture and tourism on Bolsa. In 1986 he and his partners built the $15 million Asian Garden Mall (Phước Lộc Thọ). By Clio's account, Orange County had 3,074 Vietnamese-owned businesses by 1987, and an estimated 20,000 to 50,000 people visited Bolsa Avenue on weekends.

The name was fought for. Jao tried to rebrand the area as "Asiantown" to attract a wider Asian clientele, and the effort failed. In 1988, after grassroots pressure from Vietnamese Americans, "Little Saigon" became the official name of the district bounded by Westminster Boulevard, Bolsa Avenue, Magnolia Street and Euclid Street. The name keeps alive the old name of a city that no longer officially exists. The area has also been called the "Vietnamese Nashville" for its music and media production.
keyFacts: 1978: Frank Jao opened Bridgecreek Development on Bolsa Avenue.
1986: Asian Garden Mall built for $15 million.
1987: 3,074 Vietnamese-owned businesses in Orange County, by Clio's account.
1988: "Little Saigon" made the official name after community pressure.
institutions.connectToWork: People chose "Little Saigon" over a name a developer preferred. In your materials, who decides what a place, a group or a language is called, and how would you find out what people there call it?

institutions.name: Vietnamese American Oral History Project, UC Irvine
body: Many first-generation refugees are now elderly, and their stories of war, escape, camps and resettlement could be lost. In 2011, UC Irvine's Department of Asian American Studies started the Vietnamese American Oral History Project, also known as Viet Stories, to record, preserve and share the life stories of Vietnamese Americans in Southern California.

By the project's own account, students, interns and volunteers interview community members, and the interviews are transcribed, translated, digitized and made available online. The collection is housed permanently in the UC Irvine Libraries' Southeast Asian Archive. K-12 teachers and college instructors use the stories in their classes.

It also runs exhibits and educational programs, including a 2018 exhibit at the Richard Nixon Presidential Library and Museum, and it received a Wells Fargo Foundation matching grant of up to $50,000. Its focus is Southern California, so it is background and not Minnesota history.
keyFacts: 2011: Founded by UC Irvine's Department of Asian American Studies.
Collection housed in UC Irvine Libraries' Southeast Asian Archive.
2018: Exhibit at the Richard Nixon Presidential Library and Museum.
institutions.connectToWork: If a person has lived through something your form asks about in one line, what do you need to know, and what do you not need them to retell? Who else in your process will ask them again?

institutions.name: Vietnam Assistance for the Handicapped
institutions.location: McLean, Virginia, with work in Vietnam
body: Ca Van Tran and his wife Kim founded VNAH in Virginia in 1991. James Madison University's registry confirms the 1991 founding, the McLean address and the purpose: to assist war amputees and other disabled people in Vietnam.

It began with prosthetics and wheelchairs, and over time it moved into disability policy and building services in Vietnam. Its January 2026 fact sheet lists training in social work, occupational, speech and physical therapy, vocational rehabilitation and barrier-free design. By its own account it has helped build or equip 140 schools, 40 rehabilitation units and 5 vocational schools, and it gave technical help on Vietnam's National Disability Law and on accessibility codes.
It is not a Minnesota service provider. It is an example of disability rights work started by Vietnamese Americans.
keyFacts: 1991: Founded by Ca Van Tran and Kim Tran.
By its own account, technical help on Vietnam's National Disability Law.
January 2026: Reports 85,100 people with disabilities supported.
institutions.connectToWork: What does your team know about disability rights work led by the people you serve, here or abroad? How would you learn that without asking one person to speak for everyone?

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Vietnamese Minnesotans include people who came as refugees after 1975, their U.S.-born children and grandchildren, and newer immigrants, and they are Buddhist, Catholic, other Christian, or not religious. We did not find a Minnesota study of how Vietnamese Minnesotans understand disability. What follows comes from writing about Vietnamese Americans in California, from research done in northern Vietnam, and from first-person and news accounts, and each comes with its source.
questions: How do you and your family describe what's going on, in your own words? What do you think caused it, if you want to say?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Who gave it to you, and has it helped or got in the way?
What would you want a label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Who usually helps make decisions, and who do you want involved in this one?
Who in your community may know about this, and who should not hear about it from us?
Do you get support from a temple, a church or a community group? Would you like them to be part of this, or kept out of it?
What are you already doing that helps, including prayer or traditional medicine, and is there anyone we should plan with?
Are you worried about cost, insurance or paperwork? What should we sort out first?
Would you like to talk with another Vietnamese-speaking parent or person who has been through this?
What language do you want to use with us, and what words for disability do you prefer? Which words do you want the interpreter to use?

context.heading: What has been written about explanations
body: A 2025 report from Orange County, California, by Nhien Tra Nguyen for the USC Center for Health Journalism and Nguoi Viet Daily News, says that views rooted in Buddhist and Confucian values can frame developmental differences as fate, karma or family shame, and that these views can discourage seeking help. It rests on interviews with parents and advocates, not a survey. It also says attitudes are changing, especially among younger people and families outside Vietnam.

Kim Dieu, writing for Chapman University's Thompson Policy Institute in 2018, argues against treating this as a rule. She says it is often assumed that Vietnamese Americans see disability as a debt from a past life, and that this does not describe many who have direct experience of disability. She also summarizes Huer, Saenz and Doan (2001) as finding more positive attitudes among more acculturated Vietnamese Americans, and Gammeltoft (2008), from Vietnam, as finding moral accusations against families. We know these two studies only through her summary, which does not give their samples.

Dennis Tran, an autistic Vietnamese American writing in 2022 about his own upbringing, says disability and mental health were rarely discussed and were "portrayed as a curse or bad luck." That is one person's account. Do not assume any of these explanations. Ask.

sources.label: Nhien Tra Nguyen, "Living with Autism in the Vietnamese American Community," USC Center for Health Journalism and Nguoi Viet Daily News (July 15, 2025)
Kim Dieu, "Perceptions of Disability in the Vietnamese American Community," Chapman University Thompson Policy Institute (2018)
Dennis Tran, "My Journey as a Late Autistic Diagnosed Vietnamese American Guy," Disability Belongs (2022)

context.heading: Hiding, delay and system barriers
body: In the 2025 report, Chinh Nguyen, a mother in Orange County, says families often conceal children seen as different because they fear gossip. Friends, doctors and relatives told her not to worry, or warned that an early diagnosis could bring special education and lasting stigma. Julie Diep, a speech-language pathologist who is autistic and a parent of autistic children, says people stay silent as a way to cope with bullying and social pressure.

The same report names barriers that belong to systems, not families: too few services suited to families, therapy intake that begins with cost, which Diep called "systemic abuse," and public health data that combines all Asian groups and hides what Vietnamese Americans need. Check those explanations before reading a late request for help as a matter of culture.

sources.label: Nhien Tra Nguyen, "Living with Autism in the Vietnamese American Community," USC Center for Health Journalism and Nguoi Viet Daily News (July 15, 2025)

context.heading: Family, advocacy and what helps
body: The sources we read say little about who makes decisions in Vietnamese American families with disabled members, and they do not document roles for elders or gender roles in this setting. We make no claim about them. Ask the person.

What the report does document is leadership. Chinh Nguyen serves on the board of the Regional Center of Orange County, and Diep, a school district trustee, founded the OC Autism Foundation, which the report says helps Vietnamese families get basic health care, education and lifelong services. Dieu says that contact with disabled people in families, neighborhoods and public places helps replace stereotypes with better understanding, though her post cites no study for this.

sources.label: Nhien Tra Nguyen, "Living with Autism in the Vietnamese American Community," USC Center for Health Journalism and Nguoi Viet Daily News (July 15, 2025)
Kim Dieu, "Perceptions of Disability in the Vietnamese American Community," Chapman University Thompson Policy Institute (2018)

context.heading: Words, interpreters and faith
body: We did not find a source we could rely on for the Vietnamese terms for disability, so we do not explain them here. Ask each person what words they use, and agree with a qualified interpreter beforehand which words the interpreter will use. Use trained interpreters, not children or other relatives.

Everyday English does not tell you which language someone wants for this conversation. An older adult, for example, may prefer Vietnamese even if they speak English every day, so ask. Give written materials in both plain English and Vietnamese, and check understanding by asking the person to explain the information back in their own words.

The sources we read describe faith mainly as shaping beliefs about why disability happens. They do not document traditional healing used alongside disability services, so we describe none. Asking without judgment is still reasonable.

sources.label: Nhien Tra Nguyen, "Living with Autism in the Vietnamese American Community," USC Center for Health Journalism and Nguoi Viet Daily News (July 15, 2025)
Kim Dieu, "Perceptions of Disability in the Vietnamese American Community," Chapman University Thompson Policy Institute (2018)

organizations.intro: Vietnamese Minnesotans first arrived as refugees after the fall of Saigon in 1975. MNopedia puts the population at more than 33,000 by 2023 and does not name the source of that count; the Vietnamese Community of Minnesota says over 30,000. People have organized through a mutual aid association, a social service agency, Catholic parishes, a Buddhist temple and student groups. The Vietnamese Minnesotan Museum was founded in 2025 and has a $200,000 fundraising goal. We could not find a current Vietnamese-language print paper or a Vietnamese disability organization in Minnesota. These are starting points for learning. The list is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

KFAI, Vietnam MN Radio

entries.name: Vietnamese Community of Minnesota
entries.location: Twin Cities; no permanent location, by MNopedia's account
entries.purpose: A volunteer nonprofit founded in 1981. It holds Lunar New Year and Mid-Autumn festivals, Black April commemorations and a Senior Group, and it supported the start of a Vietnamese Language School. MNopedia reports more than 20,000 people at its 2024 Lunar New Year event. As of October 2026 Tri Tang, elected in August 2023, is its president. Its 2026 Tết was held Jan. 24 and 25 at Burnsville Center. It sold its office in 2024 and moved to Brooklyn Park.

entries.name: St. Anne–St. Joseph Hien Catholic Church
entries.purpose: A parish that serves the Vietnamese Catholic community. The archdiocese lists Vietnamese Masses on Sundays, Tuesdays and Saturdays. MNopedia says St. Joseph Hien once held the only Vietnamese-language Mass in Minnesota.
entries.linkLabel: Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis listing

entries.name: St. Adalbert Catholic Church
entries.purpose: Its Vietnamese community began about 1990 (MNopedia's text says the families moved in 1989, and its chronology says December 1990), when Father Tim Kernan sponsored two families, and by 1996 about 200 families attended, by MNopedia's account. Father Minh Vu became its first Vietnamese pastor in 2001. The archdiocese lists Vietnamese Masses on Sundays and on weekdays.
entries.linkLabel: Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis listing

entries.name: Church of Saint Columba
entries.purpose: Describes itself as an English- and Vietnamese-speaking Catholic community, with a Vietnamese Mass on Sundays at 10:30 AM.

entries.name: Vietnamese Student Association of Minnesota
entries.purpose: A student group listed by the university's Asian American Studies Program. Its stated focus is Vietnamese culture on campus and in the community.
entries.linkLabel: University of Minnesota list of student organizations

entries.name: Vietnamese Minnesotans Association
entries.location: St. Paul, 1030 University Avenue West, Suite 1304
entries.purpose: A personal care assistance and home care provider. Its stated mission is the self-sufficiency and well-being of Southeast Asians, especially Vietnamese people. A summary of its IRS Form 990 filings (GrantWatch) describes a St. Paul nonprofit founded in 1993 that focuses on personal care assistance and homemaking for mostly Vietnamese American clients. It is the closest match we found to a Vietnamese-serving disability service in Minnesota.

entries.name: Vietnam MN Radio
entries.location: Minneapolis and St. Paul, on KFAI
entries.purpose: A 60-minute Vietnamese-language program covering news from Vietnam, the U.S. and the world, with arts, interviews, and discussion of health, education, immigration and law. Its most recent posted program was dated April 26, 2026. KFAI's current weekly schedule lists no Vietnamese-language program, so whether the program is still on the air is not confirmed.

entries.name: Asian American Press
entries.purpose: A pan-Asian Minnesota newspaper, begun under a company founded by Nghi Huynh in 1982. It is no longer publishing news. Its site is a digital archive that has included Vietnamese community events.

entries.name: Sahan Journal
entries.purpose: A nonprofit newsroom covering Minnesota immigrants and communities of color, including Southeast Asian communities.

entries.name: BPSOS
entries.location: Falls Church, Virginia, with offices in other states
entries.purpose: Boat People SOS began in 1980 as a volunteer rescue-at-sea effort. Its stated mission is to empower, organize and equip Vietnamese individuals and communities in their pursuit of liberty and dignity.

entries.name: Southeast Asia Resource Action Center
entries.purpose: A national civil rights organization for Cambodian, Laotian and Vietnamese Americans, founded in 1979. It works on immigration, education and health care policy and on separating Asian American data by group.

entries.name: Vietnamese American Roundtable
entries.purpose: A nonprofit built by bilingual volunteers. Programs include the SEEDS youth leadership program, Black April commemorations and festivals.

entries.name: PIVOT
entries.purpose: The Progressive Vietnamese American Organization runs VietFactCheck, VietAmVote and VietAmHealth, offering bilingual civic and health information.

entries.name: Union of North American Vietnamese Student Associations
entries.location: United States and Canada; regional unions include UVSA Midwest
entries.purpose: A leadership network for Vietnamese American students, with an annual conference.

entries.name: Người Việt
entries.purpose: Founded in 1978 by Yen Ngoc Do as a four-page weekly. Calls itself among the oldest and largest Vietnamese-language papers outside Vietnam, and it covers diaspora, U.S. and Vietnam news.

entries.name: SBTN
entries.purpose: Saigon Broadcasting Television Network, a 24-hour Vietnamese-language channel aimed at audiences outside Vietnam.

entries.name: RFA Vietnamese
entries.purpose: Radio Free Asia's Vietnamese service. RFA announced in October 2025 that it would suspend editorial operations; the Vietnamese site was posting new articles dated October 30, 2026 when checked.

entries.name: VOA Tiếng Việt
entries.purpose: Voice of America's Vietnamese service. VOA was sharply cut in 2025, and its output may be reduced; the site showed an update dated October 30, 2026 when checked.

entries.name: BBC News Tiếng Việt
entries.purpose: The BBC World Service's Vietnamese-language news service, started in 1952. Its radio broadcasts ended in 2011.
